analysis.one_liner: Forces the largest credit card issuers to enable routing over competing payment networks to lower swipe fees.
analysis.headline: The Credit Card Competition Act of 2023 never left the Senate Banking Committee — no hearing, no vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tell the Federal Reserve to bar the biggest credit card issuers — banks with over $100 billion in assets — from limiting card transactions to just one or two networks, effectively the Visa and Mastercard systems. Merchants would be able to send a card transaction over any network that can process it, which supporters say would drive down the 'swipe fee' merchants pay on every credit card sale. It also lets the Fed blacklist networks tied to foreign governments as national security risks.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants, from small shops to big chains, who pay an interchange fee on every credit card sale and could route transactions over cheaper networks. Consumers benefit indirectly if merchants pass the savings into lower prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Merchants, and consumers if prices drop

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Federal Reserve to write rules barring card issuers and networks from restricting how many networks can process a credit card transaction, and bans routing to networks affiliated with the issuer, on a national-security list, or holding the two largest market shares [S2][S3].
It prohibits issuers and networks from penalizing or inhibiting merchants who choose where to route a transaction, or pressuring them to hit volume thresholds on a particular network [S2][S3].
These rules apply only to covered issuers with more than $100 billion in assets, and do not apply to three-party systems like American Express or Discover, so smaller banks are not covered [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large banks would lose interchange-fee revenue, which they use in part to fund card rewards programs; Visa and Mastercard would lose their routing lock-in. Cardholders could see rewards trimmed or fees raised as issuers adjust.

drawbacks.text: The bill directs the Fed to make the two largest card networks ineligible as mandatory routing options, deliberately pushing transactions toward smaller networks [S3].
Rules take effect only after the Fed writes regulations, one year after enactment plus 180 days, so benefits would be delayed by rulemaking [S3].

Banks warn that cutting interchange revenue would force them to cut rewards or raise cardholder fees, and community banks that are exempt say routing volume could migrate away from their card programs anyway — a real cost an honest supporter must weigh against merchant savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a genuine bottleneck: Visa and Mastercard control routing on most cards, so merchants cannot comparison-shop for lower processing fees. If even part of the merchant savings reached shelf prices, everyday consumers would come out ahead. The main downside is uncertainty — banks would likely recoup losses through rewards cuts or new fees, which would fall hardest on cardholders who pay their balance in full, and the savings to consumers depend entirely on merchants choosing to pass them along rather than keep them.

outcome.mechanism: Durbin introduced it in June 2023 and the Senate sent it straight to the Banking Committee, which never held a markup or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Durbin (D-IL) introduced the Credit Card Competition Act of 2023 on June 7, 2023, joined by original cosponsors including Senators Roger Marshall (R-KS), J.D. Vance (R-OH), and Peter Welch (I-VT) [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S5].
That referral was the bill's last action in the 118th Congress: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote ever took place, and the Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].
The bill would have required the Federal Reserve to bar the largest card issuers from restricting transaction routing and to designate networks that pose national security risks [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and the Visa/Mastercard networks keep their routing control and interchange revenue intact; merchants and their customers continue paying the current fee structure.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Card Competition Act of 2023 and recruited bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Roger Marshall, J.D. Vance, and Peter Welch, and two other cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the outset.

for.name: Merchant and retail trade groups
for.role: Retailer coalitions such as the Merchants Payments Coalition
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for Congress to crack down on credit card swipe fees.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Sherrod Brown (D-OH) controls its agenda
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, so it never advanced to the floor.

against.name: Card networks (Visa, Mastercard)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and lobbied against similar versions of it.

against.name: Large banks and community bank trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would fund losses by cutting rewards and raising fees, and warning of spillover even to exempt smaller issuers.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — a Democratic sponsor with three Republican and two other cosponsors — but no vote was ever taken, so no party-line split appears in the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill strips their ability to lock merchants into exclusive routing, ending the two-network near-monopoly on credit card processing. Their current fees are embedded in the prices consumers pay, so their interest runs against cheaper payment options for the public.

industries.industry: Large credit card issuers (banks over $100B in assets)
industries.note: They would lose interchange revenue earned on every transaction, which funds rewards programs. Their revenue comes from fees charged through merchants, a cost ultimately reflected in consumer prices.

Merchants could route transactions over cheaper networks and could face penalties for doing so no longer. Their savings could be passed to customers through lower prices, though they are not required to.

industries.industry: Alternative payment networks (e.g., regional debit-style networks)
industries.note: By excluding the two largest networks from mandatory routing options, the bill would send transaction volume to competing networks for the first time on credit cards.

industries.industry: Smaller banks and credit unions under $100B in assets
industries.note: They are expressly exempt from the routing mandate, but they argued that card volume would still migrate away from their programs, which is why many opposed the bill despite the carve-out.
